mathematical_paraphrase: A monoid consists of a nonempty set M and an associative binary operation M×M→M together with an identity e∈M acting on both sides of each element.
mathematical_scope: A monoid need not have inverses or be commutative; the identity is required and implies nonempty carrier. Distinguish semigroups that lack identity.

term_label: binary operation (general and internally closed variants)
source_location: Binary operation definition and Also defined as
mathematical_paraphrase: A general binary operation on domains S,T with outputs in U is a map S×T→U. An internal binary operation on S is a map S×S→S; in this latter convention closure is built into the signature.
mathematical_scope: Do not silently equate arbitrary binary operations with internally closed operations. The internal convention is appropriate for monoids and groups; a general operation may have a different codomain.

source_location: Definition and Also defined as: relation as subset of Cartesian product
mathematical_paraphrase: A relation between sets S,T can be specified as an ordered triple (S,T,R) with R⊆S×T, so the typing sets are part of the object; alternatively, many texts identify the relation only with R⊆S×T. A binary relation on a single set S uses S=T.
mathematical_scope: The two formulations disagree on whether domain/codomain sets are intrinsic data; present both context-labeled variants, not as literally identical typed objects.

mathematical_paraphrase: For sets S and T, their Cartesian product S×T consists precisely of ordered pairs (s,t) with s∈S and t∈T.
mathematical_scope: Ordered pairs are set-theoretic objects; this is the binary Cartesian product, not a vector cross product. Infinite indexed Cartesian products require a separate variant.
